findings.title: Stale-tag gate compares the machine's tag against STANDBY_CONFIG_TAG while every deploy boots DEPLOY_TAG
findings.detail: The diff adds a stale-tag gate to POST /boot (index.ts:437-444): it reads `platform.statusRows().get(name)` and, when `row.status === "Running" && STANDBY_CONFIG_TAG && row.tag && row.tag !== STANDBY_CONFIG_TAG`, calls the new `platform.redeploy(name)` instead of `platform.ensure(name)`. Neither branch is exercised by any test: there is no concierge/src/index.test.ts (the /boot handler has no test file), and grep for `.redeploy(` across the repo returns only the call site at index.ts:441 — platform.test.ts covers statuses/statusRows/ensure/start/rest/waitRunning/awaitDns but never constructs a Platform and calls `redeploy`, so the new interface member (platform.ts:49), its tinfoil implementation (platform.ts:282-285), its docker stub (platform.ts:108), and the `rest(...).catch(() => undefined)` swallow in it are all untested. This branch is the one that decides to stop-and-redeploy a live machine based on a tag comparison; a regression in the condition (e.g. inverted equality, missing STANDBY_CONFIG_TAG guard) would either never redeploy stale machines or redeploy healthy ones, and nothing would fail.
findings.recommendation: Compare against the tag the deploy path actually uses (`const expected = DEPLOY_TAG || STANDBY_CONFIG_TAG`) — the same value passed to createPlatform — and log the expected tag from that variable.

findings.title: New JWT-accepting /handshake branch and k=1 /handoff/pull fallback ship with no test protection
findings.detail: Still valid. /handshake remains a two-tier resolver — verified bb JWT → users.rebind(id.sub), 409 on presented_instance ≠ resolved (index.ts:487-509), then the secret tier — and /handoff/pull still carries the k=1 legacy fallback. `find concierge/src/*.test.ts` yields only auth/handoff/platform/pool/postbox/table/user-machines tests; there is no route-level test for index.ts and no test references /handshake or /handoff/pull (server/src/concierge.test.ts only covers the client side). A regression in the rebind branch, the inverted 409 check, the legacyCaller gate or the ambiguity denial would pass CI silently.
findings.recommendation: Add a concierge route test (stub verifyExternal/users/handoff) asserting: JWT + matching presented_instance mints; mismatch → 409; rebind null → 404; secret tier unchanged; /handoff/pull serves only the single open window and denies when k>1.

findings.title: /handoff/pull k=1 fallback serves a fired machine's escrowed master secret to any shared-secret holder
findings.detail: The /handoff/pull route (line 597) authorizes with `allowedInstance(instance)` + `requireSecret(req, reply)`. requireSecret only checks the fleet-wide shared secret (CONCIERGE_TOKEN, index.ts:61/278) — the same value every machine and any secret holder presents. When the exact-name `handoff.release(instance)` returns notFound, a caller whose instance name is in neither the user (`USER_NAME_RE`) nor standby (`STANDBY_NAME_RE`) namespace (e.g. the operator's static ALLOWED name "waddle", index.ts:64-65) takes the legacy branch (index.ts:611-616): `handoff.singleOpenWindow()` (handoff.ts:107) yields the one armed instance with an open fire window, and `release(open)` returns its credential. That credential is the machine-parked opaque bag `{ secret, schedules[], snapshot? }` — the user's master secret (see /handoff doc, index.ts:565) — and it is returned wholesale in the 200 body. So any shared-secret holder, while a *different* user's machine is in its ~3-minute schedule-boot release window, can pull and obtain that user's master secret. The code comment itself flags this as the accepted k=1 seam; it is a real cross-tenant secret disclosure, not merely a logging concern.
findings.recommendation: Bind the fallback to the caller identity rather than the shared key alone (require the concierge-minted session/instance the puller was deployed for, or a pull marker minted at deploy time), or drop the fallback now that machines adopt their name from /handshake.

findings.title: wakeCore's DEV branch is a dead end that reports a failure without attempting anything
findings.detail: Superseded by the current code: the DEV branch polls the already-running dev agent (pollUntilHealthy, 30 attempts) and only then reports failure, rather than falling through to an unconditional failure note. Residual, non-robustness drift remains: the doc block above still claims the legacy primary /wake 'is the whole story in dev parity', which the DEV branch no longer does (it never POSTs /wake).
findings.recommendation: Update the stale dev-parity comment; no code change needed for the reported dead-end.

findings.title: Auto-discovery now fires on every verification failure, contradicting the retained comment and its stop-and-redeploy guard
findings.detail: Resolved by this diff: the new `if (!activeEnclave)` branch plus the retained unreachability probe (fetch with AbortSignal.timeout(2500)) mean a machine that answers /health but fails verification/config no longer triggers a /boot. The guard the prior finding said was bypassed is back in place, and the comment now matches the behavior.

findings.title: New first-load discovery branch in run() is untested — App.tsx has no test file
findings.detail: The diff adds `if (!activeEnclave) { void wakeCore("no machine yet — discovering"); return; }` (App.tsx:214-217) inside run()'s catch, changing the first-load failure path from 'show the error screen' to 'kick off discovery'. Client tests exist only for lib/hooks (background, bb-grant, concierge, history, use-once-answer); there is no App.test.tsx and grep for `wakeCore`/`activeEnclave`/`discoveryTried` finds no test references, so this new branch, the unreachable-probe branch it precedes, and the `discoveryTriedRef` loop guard that is supposed to bound them are all unexercised. A regression that drops the ref check would loop discovery indefinitely with no failing test to catch it.
findings.recommendation: Extract the catch-branch decision (unreachable-only vs no-machine-yet, guarded by discoveryTriedRef) into a pure helper and unit-test it, or add a component test that mocks verifyEnclave/fetch to assert wakeCore is called exactly once on first-load failure.

findings.title: k=1 fallback consumes the one-shot fire for any allowed shared-secret caller
findings.detail: The same legacy branch calls `handoff.release(open)` (index.ts:614), and release() deletes `firedAt.delete(instance)` on success (handoff.ts:132) — the fire is one-shot. Because the fallback caller is identified only by the fleet secret plus a non-dynamic name, ANY shared-secret holder (not the intended just-deployed machine) can win the race and consume the fire. The intended schedule-boot's own subsequent pull then gets `notFound` and 404, so it stays a locked ceremony and the unattended boot silently fails — an availability/authz failure distinct from disclosure. The route comment (index.ts:594-596) assumes the puller is the fire's intended boot; the fallback breaks that assumption.
findings.recommendation: Make the fallback non-consuming on a duplicate/unsuccessful attempt (do not clear the fire until the intended boot confirms), and/or require a pull marker minted at deploy time.

findings.title: currentInstance() is exported but unused, and its doc comment contradicts the actual AAD source
findings.detail: Resolved: the comment no longer claims any v1 AAD fallback for currentInstance(), and no production seal/open site consumes it (only concierge.test.ts), which the comment now states. The described contradiction is gone.

findings.title: Transient handshake failure is indistinguishable from an identity refusal and now leaves the machine with no concierge session
findings.detail: Still valid: `if (bb?.token && instance) return (await handshakeConcierge(bb.token, instance)) ? bb.token : undefined;` treats a transient blip the same as the concierge's deliberate 409, so bearer is undefined, renewIdleStop() (line 324) is skipped and the machine arms no stop/wake rows for the session, with no retry and no distinct log line.
findings.recommendation: Distinguish transport/5xx failures from a definitive 409 in handshakeConcierge (or the caller) and retry/log them separately.
